# Proof that zeta(2) = sum 1/n^2 = pi^2/6

For real s > 1, zeta(s) = sum_{n>=1} n^{-s}; so zeta(2) is the series sum 1/n^2. Let S_N = sum_{n=1}^N 1/n^2. We show S_N -> pi^2/6.

**Step 1 (elementary inequalities).** For 0 < x < pi/2: sin x < x < tan x.
Let f(x) = x - sin x, g(x) = tan x - x on [0, pi/2). f(0)=g(0)=0, f'(x) = 1 - cos x > 0 and g'(x) = sec^2 x - 1 = tan^2 x > 0 for 0 < x < pi/2. By the mean value theorem f, g are strictly increasing on [0, pi/2), hence positive on (0, pi/2).
Since all quantities are positive, squaring and inverting gives
cot^2 x = 1/tan^2 x < 1/x^2 < 1/sin^2 x = 1 + cot^2 x.   (1)

**Step 2 (a trigonometric sum).** Fix an integer m >= 1 and put theta_k = k pi/(2m+1), k = 1, ..., m. Then
sum_{k=1}^m cot^2 theta_k = m(2m-1)/3.   (2)

By de Moivre (integer exponent 2m+1), cos((2m+1)theta) + i sin((2m+1)theta) = (cos theta + i sin theta)^{2m+1}. Expanding by the binomial theorem and taking imaginary parts (the terms with odd power 2j+1 of i sin theta, where i^{2j+1} = (-1)^j i):
sin((2m+1)theta) = sum_{j=0}^m (-1)^j C(2m+1, 2j+1) cos^{2m-2j} theta sin^{2j+1} theta.
If sin theta != 0 this equals sin^{2m+1} theta * P(cot^2 theta), where
P(t) = sum_{j=0}^m (-1)^j C(2m+1, 2j+1) t^{m-j}.
For theta = theta_k (1 <= k <= m) we have 0 < theta_k < pi/2, so sin theta_k != 0, while sin((2m+1)theta_k) = sin(k pi) = 0. Hence P(cot^2 theta_k) = 0 for k = 1, ..., m.
On (0, pi/2), cot is positive and strictly decreasing, so cot^2 theta_1 > cot^2 theta_2 > ... > cot^2 theta_m > 0 are m distinct roots of P. P has degree exactly m with leading coefficient C(2m+1,1) = 2m+1 != 0, so these are all its roots, and P(t) = (2m+1) prod_k (t - cot^2 theta_k). Comparing coefficients of t^{m-1} (Vieta): the coefficient of t^{m-1} in P is -C(2m+1,3), and in the product it is -(2m+1) sum_k cot^2 theta_k, so
sum_k cot^2 theta_k = C(2m+1,3)/(2m+1) = (2m+1)(2m)(2m-1)/(6(2m+1)) = m(2m-1)/3.

**Step 3 (squeeze).** Apply (1) with x = theta_k in (0, pi/2) and sum over k = 1..m. Using (2) and 1/theta_k^2 = (2m+1)^2/(pi^2 k^2):
m(2m-1)/3 < ((2m+1)^2/pi^2) S_m < m(2m-1)/3 + m = 2m(m+1)/3.
Multiplying by pi^2/(2m+1)^2 > 0:
pi^2 * m(2m-1) / (3(2m+1)^2) < S_m < pi^2 * 2m(m+1) / (3(2m+1)^2).
As m -> infinity, m(2m-1)/(2m+1)^2 -> 2/4 = 1/2 and 2m(m+1)/(2m+1)^2 -> 2/4 = 1/2, so both bounds tend to pi^2/6. By the squeeze theorem S_m -> pi^2/6. Hence the series converges and
zeta(2) = sum_{n=1}^infty 1/n^2 = pi^2/6. QED
